title: Socket and plug: one shared package, two apps
subtitle: How an abstract class + get_it lets each app plug in its own SDK. Worked example: the Crashlytics split from the Measure work (cb7038e3).

meta.description: Why an SDK in services ships in both apps, the abstract class as a socket, each app's plug with @LazySingleton(as:), the generated registration, module order in injector.dart, and how shared code receives the right plug.

actors.name: The app
actors.explain: Each app lists in its pubspec which packages it uses. Ultra lists ultra_services, never bonds_services, and the reverse.

actors.name: injector.dart
actors.explain: Each app's DI setup. It says which packages register their classes, and in what order.

actors.name: get_it
actors.explain: A global map from 'type' to 'how to build it'. Code asks get_it for a type and gets whatever was registered for it.

actors.name: bonds_services
actors.explain: Bonds-only package. Holds the implementations that use Firebase Crashlytics, Firebase Performance, Cronet…

actors.name: ultra_services
actors.explain: Ultra-only package. Holds the implementations that use Measure (and the 'no native adapter' plug).

actors.name: services
actors.explain: Shared by both apps. Holds abstract classes (the sockets) and the code that uses them, but no app-specific SDK.

actors.name: Shared code
actors.explain: Any class in services that needs the feature, e.g. the native adapter's fallback logging a Crashlytics error.

steps.title: Who's who in a split
steps.summary: The idea: the shared package only describes WHAT it needs (a socket). Each app's own package provides HOW (a plug). get_it connects them at startup, and each app only ever sees its own plugs.
steps.oneliner: Socket in services, plug in the app's package, get_it as the wire.
steps.boardHint: Press Next → to see the problem this solves.

steps.title: The problem: what's in services ships in both apps
steps.summary: Before the Measure work, CrashlyticsService was a real Firebase class inside services, and firebase_crashlytics was in services' pubspec. Both apps depend on services, so both apps shipped Firebase Crashlytics, even ultra, which wanted Measure instead.
steps.oneliner: A dependency of a dependency still ends up in your APK.

messages.label: depends on services
messages.why: New term: transitive dependency. Ultra never asked for Firebase Crashlytics, but it asked for services, and services asked for Firebase. So it arrives anyway. In Gradle terms: services exposed it like an api(…) dependency.

notes.30: Firebase Crashlytics, in the shared package.

messages.label: uses concrete Firebase class
messages.why: The class itself imported Firebase. Anyone using CrashlyticsService was tied to Firebase, with no way for ultra to swap it.

notes.3: The SDK import lives in the shared package.
notes.10: A concrete class: there's exactly one way it works.

steps.title: The socket: an abstract class
steps.summary: After the split, services keeps only a description of the feature: an abstract class with method signatures and no code. No SDK import. Shared code depends on this description, not on Firebase or Measure.
steps.oneliner: The socket says 'something that can record an error'. It doesn't care who.

messages.label: recordCrashlyticsError()
messages.why: New term: abstract class. Like a Kotlin interface: it lists what must exist, without implementing it. You can't create one directly; you can only hold a reference to 'something that implements it'.

notes.1: abstract: a contract, not a class you can build.
notes.2: Just the signature. No body, no Firebase, no Measure.

steps.title: The plugs: one implementation per app
steps.summary: Each app's own package implements the socket with its own SDK. Bonds' plug uses Firebase Crashlytics; ultra's uses Measure. The SDK line moves into that package's pubspec, so only that app gets it.
steps.oneliner: Same socket shape, different wiring inside. The SDK travels with the plug.

messages.label: FirebaseCrashlyticsService implements
messages.why: New term: implements. 'I promise to provide every method the abstract class lists', like `class X : MyInterface` in Kotlin. The compiler checks the promise.

notes.10: Fills the socket's contract with Firebase code.

messages.label: MeasureCrashlyticsService implements
messages.why: Same socket, completely different SDK inside. services can't tell the difference, and doesn't need to.

messages.label: SDK lives in this pubspec
messages.why: measure_flutter is listed here, not in services. Only apps that depend on ultra_services (i.e. ultra) get it. Bonds' pubspec has firebase_crashlytics the same way.

notes.14: Depends on services, to see the socket.
notes.18: The SDK, now only in ultra's tree.

steps.title: Registration: the annotation writes the wiring
steps.summary: @LazySingleton(as: CrashlyticsService) is an instruction to the code generator (injectable). When you run melos generate, it writes a module file that tells get_it: 'when someone asks for CrashlyticsService, build a FirebaseCrashlyticsService'.
steps.oneliner: You write the annotation; build_runner writes the registration; get_it stores it.

messages.label: lazySingleton<CrashlyticsService>
messages.why: New term: lazy singleton. Built once, on first use, then reused. Like Hilt's @Singleton + Lazy<T>. The generated file is gitignored, so this peek shows the one on your disk.

notes.23: The socket type is the key…
notes.25: …and the plug is the value. gh<…>() inside the lambda runs later, on first use.
notes.28: The native adapter split uses exactly the same shape.

steps.title: Startup: each app plugs in only its own package
steps.summary: Each app's injector.dart lists the modules to register, in order: its own per-app package first, then services, then common. Ultra's lists UltraServicesPackageModule; it has no way to even see bonds_services.
steps.oneliner: The app chooses the plugs simply by which package it lists.

messages.label: configureInjection()
messages.why: Called once in main() before the app runs. Like setting up a Hilt component before any Activity starts.

messages.label: register ultra plugs, then services
messages.why: Why the plugs must be lazy: they register BEFORE services, so things they need (PreferenceService, DiagnosticLogger) don't exist yet. A lazy plug is only built later, when first asked for, by which point everything is registered.

steps.title: Shared code asks for the socket, gets the app's plug
steps.summary: Code in services only ever names the socket type. get_it hands it whichever plug the running app registered. In bonds that's Firebase; in ultra it's Measure. Same line of shared code, different behaviour per app.
steps.oneliner: Shared code depends on the socket. Each app decides the plug. That's the whole trick.

messages.label: give me a CrashlyticsService
messages.why: New term: dependency inversion. The shared code depends on an abstraction (the socket), and the concrete choice is made outside, by the app. Usually via a constructor parameter that injectable fills in.

messages.label: this app's plug
messages.why: Ultra resolves it explicitly at startup, too, so its error handlers are installed even if nothing else asks first.

notes.36: Ask by socket type. Ultra gets Measure here; bonds' same line gets Firebase.
